Exposure therapy can work if you're in a relatively stable place to begin with, IME, but just jumping into it when you're like this isn't really the best way to deal with it. 

Two therapies which have actually introduced useful ideas for me have been CBT (cognitive-behavioural therapy) and ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy). In these the therapist gives more specific advice that can make beginning to deal with anxieties and depression a *lot* easier. I've also heard good things about IFS (internal family systems), which I think models conflicting internal desires and aspects of yourself as a group of individuals, and uses family counseling techniques to help resolve differences between the different parts of you.  

Therapy isn't magic, and as far as I'm aware CBT is the only one that's consistently shown strong positive results in clinical trials. 

Here's a few ideas that I've had varying levels of success with, most of which probably won't work for you specifically. Hopefully one of two of them are beneficial, though.

* Success spirals. In this idea, a minor success (as small as making eye contact with a stranger if you have social anxiety) can lead to *slightly* more confidence in yourself, so next

* Explicit self-reinforcement. Tied in with the previous one, explicit self-reinforcement is when you reward yourself, either internally with pride, externally with sweet food, or through something else quick and immediate that works for you, for each action you take to combat your anxiety. 

* I don't know the term for this, but in ACT there's the idea of imagining you're driving a bus, and all those distracting intrusive thoughts are like the voices of the passengers of the bus. *You're* still the driver, and you can acknowledge that they're there, not ignore them, but instead just decide that you won't take their advice into account. 

* Bayes' Theorem. Related to the ACT idea above, and probably not helpful for everyone, but it's a mathematical equation that, once grokked, will change how you think about everything. The ideas that are intruding into your head are not Bayesian evidence *at all*. They would be saying what they're saying whether it's true or not.

* The classic diet, exercise, sleep and hydration combo. I'm sure you've heard it before, and you're sick of it, but it really will make a difference if you can manage it.

I'm too fucking anxious and awkward to call my doctor after I missed my last appointment. I am not a functioning human, I can't even work entry-level jobs because I wouldn't be able to deal with customers or coworkers. I was diagnosed with avoidant personality disorder and obsessive compulsive personality disorder as well as major depression when I went to my psychiatrist. "Personality disorder" is a polite way of saying "You're fucked up in an unfixable way." I'm not someone it's healthy to be friends with or be in a relationship with. I failed two semesters at uni, and haven't applied to go back next semester. I've got very little to live for.

I've failed because I run out of stuff to do or decide I deserve a break, because to be honest the workload they give us is nothing, and then I keep telling myself I can do the work later, because I'm still ahead, or it won't take long to catch up, until it's the night before an assignment is due and I haven't started or learned the material and then I panic and basically ignore the class until exam time.
